C13724 (5.1.1(a)) requires the ACPE to limit unintended acceleration when a misapplication is detected and an obstacle is ahead with forward direction selected. This matches the product function.
C13724 (5.1.1(b)) requires the same limiting when an obstacle is behind and rearward direction is selected. The product detects obstacles behind the vehicle.

C13725 (5.1.2) defines misapplication as pedal velocity of at least 400 %/s over at least 70 % of travel, reaching at least 90 % position. The numbers are preserved and the product detects sudden, strong pedal input.

C13726 (5.1.3) applies only to systems that implement force-based triggering. The specification only says 'sudden, strong accelerator pedal input' and does not state whether triggering is force-based, so applicability cannot be determined.

The requirement to justify the triggering threshold in C13726 (5.1.3) applies only if force-based triggering is implemented. The product's triggering principle is not specified, so applicability is undetermined.
C13727 (5.1.4) requires the ACPE to control acceleration when the vehicle accelerates from standstill. This is supported and applicable.

C13728 (5.1.4.1) requires a driver indication if the ACPE is not ready 6 s after powertrain initiation, persisting until initialisation succeeds. The product has an instrument cluster tell-tale and reports faults.
C13729 (5.1.5) sets the 1.0–1.5 m obstacle distance requirement together with the conditions in (a)–(d). The conditions are preserved and the requirement is supported and applicable.
C13729 (5.1.5, final paragraph) requires that the system does not deactivate or unreasonably switch control strategy when conditions deviate. This is a supported performance obligation.

C13729 requires the manufacturer to demonstrate non-deactivation under deviating conditions per Annex 3, with optional Technical Service testing if justified. This is a necessary verification obligation. Annex 3 content is not supplied and the dependency remains explicit.

C13730 (5.1.6) limits the collision speed to no more than 8 km/h above the vehicle speed at the point where the 5.1.2 triggering conditions are met, if a collision is not prevented. This is supported.
C13730 (5.1.6) also limits the collision speed to no more than 70 % of the speed without ACPE intervention. This is supported.

C13731 (5.1.6.1) sets a minimum 15 % speed reduction where 30 % cannot be achieved due to a low power-to-test-mass ratio and the vehicle does not exceed 8 km/h without ACPE. The conditions are preserved.

C13732 (5.1.7) requires acceleration to continue to be limited during any intervention. It only permits ending the intervention when the obstacle is no longer detected or the driver interrupts. The word 'only' converts a permission into an exclusive restriction that the source does not state.
C13732 (5.1.7) requires the manufacturer to declare the ACPE continuation conditions to the technical service. This is a supported declaration tied to the system's engineering behaviour.
C13733 (5.1.8) requires that ACPE effectiveness is not adversely affected by magnetic or electrical fields. This applies to the electronic system.

Annex 16 1.2 requires testing per IEC 61000-4-5 Clause 4.2 for lightning transients, unless the Annex states otherwise.

Annex 16 2.1.1 requires the vehicle to be immobilized, with the engine(s) OFF and in charging mode.

Annex 16 2.1.2 requires other vehicle systems that can affect immunity-related functions to be tested in a way agreed between manufacturer and Technical Service. This is relevant to the ACPE and powertrain control functions. The test method itself is not specified in the source.

Annex 16 2.1.2 requires the REESS to be in charging mode with traction battery SOC between 20% and 80% of maximum SOC for the whole measurement duration. For multiple batteries the average SOC is considered.

Annex 16 2.1.2 sets the charging current conditions if current consumption can be adjusted. AC charging: at least 20% of maximum rated charging/input current. DC charging: at least 20% of nominal value, or a minimum of 16 A if 20% cannot be achieved in the test facility, unless another value is agreed with the Type Approval Authorities.

Annex 16 2.1.2 lists the failure criteria: vehicle sets in motion, unexpected release of the parking brake, and loss of park position for an automatic transmission. The product is an automatic transmission vehicle, so these criteria apply.

Annex 16 2.2 requires only non-perturbing monitoring equipment, and monitoring of the vehicle exterior and passenger compartment to determine whether the Annex requirements are met.

UN R155 4.4 requires the approval mark on or close to the manufacturer's vehicle data plate.

7.3.5 applies to the vehicle type and is conditional ('if provided'). The condition is preserved in the requirement, so it is kept as a conditional obligation.
7.3.6 requires pre-approval testing to verify the effectiveness of the security measures. This is a necessary engineering test and applies to the M1/N1 vehicle type.

7.3.7(b) requires measures supporting the manufacturer's monitoring capability. It is supported by the source and applies to the vehicle type.
7.3.7(c) requires data forensic capability. It is supported by the source and applies to the vehicle type.

Reporting and confirming mitigation effectiveness to the Approval Authority is an administrative procedure. It is not a product engineering obligation.
8.1 notification of modifications to the approval authority is an administrative approval procedure. It does not constrain the product itself.
9.1 requires conformity of production procedures to comply with the 1958 Agreement Schedule 1. This constrains manufacturing conformity and applies to the approved M1/N1 type.

Annex 5 para 2 requires Parts A, B and C to be considered in risk assessment and mitigations. It is source-supported and applies to the vehicle type including the ACPE.
Annex 5 para 4 requires the threat analysis to consider possible attack impacts, and the listed impacts are preserved. It is source-supported and applicable.
Table A1 mitigation M10 requires the vehicle to verify the authenticity and integrity of the messages it receives. The ACPE uses in-vehicle communication, so it applies.

Mitigation M12 requires protection of confidential data transmitted to or from the vehicle. The requirement is conditional on such transmission, and the product facts do not specify it, so it is kept with its condition.
Mitigation M13 requires measures to detect and recover from denial of service attacks. It is source-supported and applies to the vehicle and its networks.
Mitigation M9 requires measures to prevent and detect unauthorized access, including privilege escalation. It is source-supported and applies to the ACPE control unit.
Mitigation M16 requires secure software update procedures. It is conditional on the ACPE software being updatable, and the condition is preserved.

Mitigation M11 requires security controls for storing cryptographic keys. The requirement is conditional on keys being used for software updates, which the product facts do not specify, so it is kept with its condition.
Mitigation M18 requires defining and controlling user roles and access privileges based on least privilege. It is source-supported and applies to the vehicle systems.
Mitigation M21 requires software to be security assessed, authenticated and integrity protected. It applies to the ACPE software in the powertrain control unit and to the infotainment menu.
Mitigation M21 requires security controls to minimise the risk from third-party software that is intended or foreseeably hosted on the vehicle. The condition from the source is preserved.
Mitigation M22 requires security controls on external interfaces. The requirement is conditional on such interfaces existing, which the product facts do not specify, so it is kept with its condition.
Table A1 threats 19.1 and 20.1 map to mitigation M7, which requires access control to protect system data and code. The ACPE software sits in the powertrain control unit, so it is in scope.
Threat 19.3 maps to M11, which requires security controls for storing cryptographic keys. It is correctly framed as conditional on the ACPE using keys, which the product facts do not specify.

Threats 20.5, 21.1 and 25.1 map to M7. Access control applies to diagnostic data, event logs and configuration parameters of key functions. The ACPE is a driver-assistance function that intervenes in propulsion torque, so this is applicable.
Threat 24.1 maps to M13, which requires measures to detect and recover from denial of service, such as CAN flooding. The ACPE ECU is on the internal network, so this applies.
Threats 26.1-26.3 and 27.1 map to M23, which requires cybersecurity best practices for software and hardware development. The proposal is supported and applicable.

Threats 28.1 and 28.2 map to M23 and require cybersecurity testing with adequate coverage. This covers software bugs and development remainders such as debug and JTAG ports. It is supported and applicable.

Threats 29.1 and 29.2 map to M23 and require best practices for system design and integration. These address open ports and unprotected gateways. The ACPE is an integrated, networked system, so this applies.

Threat 31.1 maps to M24, which requires best practices for protecting the integrity and confidentiality of stored personal data. It is correctly conditional on personal data being stored, which the product facts do not specify.
Threat 32.1 maps to M9, which requires measures to prevent and detect unauthorized access against manipulation of OEM hardware. It is applicable to the ACPE hardware: ECU, sensors and links.

UN R156 7.1.2 requires the manufacturer to record and store information for each update applied to a vehicle type. It is conditional on updates being applied. The ACPE software in the powertrain control unit is software that could be updated, so this applies.
R156 7.1.2.1 requires documentation of the software update processes and of any standards used to demonstrate compliance. It sits under the 7.1.2 record-and-store obligation and is supported.

R156 7.1.2.2 requires documentation of the configuration of relevant type-approved systems before and after an update, including hardware and software identification and versions and relevant parameters. It is supported.
R156 7.1.2.3 requires an auditable register per RXSWIN, covering software versions and integrity validation data before and after an update. It is conditional on RXSWIN use and is supported.
R156 7.1.2.4 requires documentation listing the target vehicles for the update and confirming that their last known configuration is compatible with it. It is supported.
R156 7.1.2.5 (a)-(i) lists the required documentation content for all software updates of the vehicle type. The proposal preserves all items and is supported.

R156 7.1.3.1 requires the manufacturer to demonstrate a process that protects software updates against manipulation before the update starts. It constrains the update engineering process and is supported.
R156 7.1.3.2 requires the manufacturer to demonstrate that the update processes, including development of the update delivery system, are protected against compromise. It is supported.

R156 7.1.3.3 requires the manufacturer to demonstrate that the processes for verifying and validating software functionality and code are appropriate. It is supported and applies to the ACPE software.
R156 7.2.1.1 requires the authenticity and integrity of software updates to be protected so as to reasonably prevent compromise and invalid updates. It is supported.
R156 7.2.1.2.1 requires each RXSWIN to be uniquely identifiable. It is conditional on the vehicle type using RXSWIN and is supported.

R156 7.2.1.2.1 requires the RXSWIN to be updated when type-approval-relevant software is modified by the manufacturer and the modification leads to a type approval extension or a new type approval. It is conditional on RXSWIN use and is supported.

R156 7.2.1.2.2 requires each RXSWIN to be readable in a standardized way via the OBD port. It includes the alternative where RXSWINs are not held on the vehicle: declare software versions to the Approval Authority and keep the declaration updated. This is a single obligation with a conditional branch, not duplicated routes, and it is supported.

R156 7.2.1.2.3 requires the manufacturer to protect RXSWINs and/or software versions on the vehicle against unauthorised modification. It is supported. The confidential provision of the protection means at type approval is an administrative addition and is not needed in the engineering obligation.
